study.title: Probability and random-variable notation
study.locator: Chapter 2, Sections 2.1-2.2.2 (pp. 33-38): events, the conditional-probability definition, discrete and continuous variables, CDFs and quantiles

focus: The naive definition needs finite and equally likely outcomes. State both assumptions before counting.
A PMF gives probabilities that sum to 1. A density does not: only its integral over a set is a probability, and a density value can exceed 1.
The CDF \(F(x)=P(X \le x)\) works for every variable type and determines the distribution.
Universality: for continuous \(X\) with CDF \(F\), \(F(X)\) is \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). This is the seed of inverse-CDF sampling in the transforms unit.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, count \(P(\text{sum of two fair dice}=9)=4/36=1/9\) from the 36 ordered pairs. Then check with NumPy in float64: numpy.random.default_rng(7), a (200000, 2) int64 array from integers(1, 7); the fraction of sums equal to 9 is 0.11259 with standard error 0.00071, within about 2 standard errors of 1/9.
traps: Reading a density value as a probability. For continuous \(X\), \(P(X=x)=0\); report \(P(X \in \text{an interval})\) instead.
Calling an outcome random without a distribution. Name the set, the probabilities on it and the sampling scheme.
Assuming distinct-looking formulas give distinct distributions. Compare the CDF or the PMF values, which settle identity.

selfTest.q: Two dice: why is \(P(\text{sum }9)=4/36\) and not 4/11?
selfTest.a: Sums 2 to 12 are 11 values but not equally likely, so the naive definition does not apply to them. The 36 ordered pairs are equally likely by symmetry of fair independent dice, and 4 of them sum to 9. The step that uses the assumption is choosing the 36 pairs as the counting set.

selfTest.q: Give a density that exceeds 1 somewhere and show it is still valid.
selfTest.a: \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0, 0.5)\) has density 2 on its support and integrates to 1. Validity uses non-negativity plus integral 1; no step bounds the density pointwise.

selfTest.q: \(X\) is continuous with strictly increasing CDF \(F\). Prove \(F(X)\) is \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\), naming each assumption.
selfTest.a: \(P(F(X) \le u)=P(X \le F^{-1}(u))\) uses strict increase for the inverse step, then equals \(F(F^{-1}(u))=u\) by continuity of \(F\). The result \(u\) on \((0,1)\) is the Uniform CDF.

selfTest.q: A learner simulates 2000 dice pairs, gets 0.125, and claims the exact answer is wrong. What is the error?
selfTest.a: Simulation noise. The standard error is \(\sqrt{(1/9)(8/9)/2000}=0.0070\), so 0.125 sits 1.98 standard errors above 1/9, a gap about one run in 20 produces. A simulation reports an estimate with its standard error; it never refutes an exact count.

study.title: Chain rule and conditional independence
study.locator: Chapter 2, Sections 2.1.3.4-2.1.3.6 and 2.2.3-2.2.4 (pp. 35, 38-40): conditional probability, product and chain rules, independence and conditional independence

focus: \(P(A \mid B)=P(A,B)/P(B)\) restricts the sample space to \(B\). Write the restricted space before computing.
The chain rule factors any joint distribution. An independence claim drops a conditioning bar and must be justified, never assumed silently.
Conditioning can reverse a comparison, as Simpson examples show. Report the conditioning set with every rate.
Monty Hall rewards writing the host protocol as a conditional distribution, not as unconditional door odds.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive \(P(\text{both boys} \mid \text{at least one boy})=1/3\): the reduced space {BB, BG, GB} is equally likely and one outcome in three is BB. Check with NumPy in float64: numpy.random.default_rng(11), a (300000, 2) array from integers(0, 2) with 1 coding a boy; the conditional fraction is 0.33357 over 225364 conditioned pairs, with standard error 0.00099.
traps: Swapping \(P(A \mid B)\) with \(P(B \mid A)\). Write both conditionals with their different denominators.
Reading pairwise independence as mutual independence. A three-coin Bernstein-style construction breaks it by hand.
Confusing conditional with marginal independence in either direction. The chess problem in Strategic Practice 2 (Q5, given the opponent's skill level) separates the two.

selfTest.q: Derive Bayes rule from the definition of conditional probability and name the step that needs \(P(B)>0\).
selfTest.a: \(P(A \mid B)=P(A,B)/P(B)\) and \(P(B \mid A)=P(A,B)/P(A)\); eliminating \(P(A,B)\) gives \(P(A \mid B)=P(B \mid A)P(A)/P(B)\). Division needs \(P(B)>0\), and expanding \(P(B)\) by total probability needs a partition of the space.

selfTest.q: Two fair coins. Are {first is heads} and {at least one head} independent?
selfTest.a: No. \(P(\text{first H})=1/2\) and \(P(\text{at least one H})=3/4\), so independence needs \(P(\text{both})=3/8\). The intersection is {first is heads} itself, {HH, HT}, with probability 1/2.

selfTest.q: Give variables that are conditionally independent given \(Z\) but marginally dependent.
selfTest.a: Two symptoms given disease status: given \(Z\) they are independent by the modeling assumption, but unconditionally they correlate through the unobserved common cause \(Z\).

selfTest.q: In Reproduce, why is the answer 1/3 and not 1/2?
selfTest.a: Conditioning on at least one boy leaves {BB, BG, GB}, three equally likely outcomes. The 1/2 answer conditions on a different event, namely that a specified child is a boy.

study.title: Moments and the total laws
study.locator: Chapter 2, Section 2.2.5 (pp. 40-43): mean, linearity, variance, law of total expectation and law of total variance with the mixture example

focus: Linearity of expectation needs no independence. The variance of a sum needs uncorrelatedness; independence is sufficient, not necessary.

Eve's law splits variance into explained plus residual: \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X])+\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X)]\). Name which term each modeling choice changes.
Taking out what is known, \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)Y \mid X]=g(X)\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\), needs \(g(X)\) fixed given \(X\). Conditioning on the wrong variable breaks it.
Zero correlation with clear dependence is one construction away: take \(X \sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, 1)\) and \(Y=X^2\), then \(\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=\mathbb{E}[X^3]=0\) by symmetry.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive Eve's law on a two-stage model: with probability 1/2 roll a fair die (mean 3.5, variance 35/12) and otherwise take 10. Then \(\mathbb{E}[X]=6.75\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=35/24+(10-3.5)^2/4=12.0208\): the first term uses LOTUS on the die branch and the second uses \(\operatorname{Var}\) of \(\{3.5, 10\}\). Check with NumPy in float64: numpy.random.default_rng(21), n = 400000, branch I from integers(0, 2) and then the die from integers(1, 7), with I = 0 taking the die value and I = 1 taking 10; sample mean 6.7493 and variance 12.023 with standard error of the mean 0.00548.
traps: Pushing a nonlinear function inside an expectation. \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\) differs from \(g(\mathbb{E}[X])\); Jensen fixes the direction for convex \(g\).
Dropping the covariance term in \(\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)\) without checking uncorrelatedness first.
Quoting a conditional expectation as a number. \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\) is a function of \(X\); only \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X=x]\) is a number.

selfTest.q: Prove Eve's law from the definition of variance, naming where each assumption is used.
selfTest.a: Write \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}[Y^2]-\mathbb{E}[Y]^2\), then condition: \(\mathbb{E}[Y^2]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y^2 \mid X]]\) by Adam's law, which needs \(\mathbb{E}|Y^2|\) finite. Subtract \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]]^2\) after writing \(\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]]\) by the same law, and regroup into \(\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X)]+\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X])\). Both steps use iterated expectation, hence integrability.

selfTest.q: \(X \sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, 1)\) and \(Y=X^2\). Show \(\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=0\) while \(X\) and \(Y\) are dependent. Why is symmetry alone not enough?
selfTest.a: \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\mathbb{E}[X^3]=0\) by symmetry and \(\mathbb{E}[X]=0\), so \(\operatorname{Cov}=0\). Dependence: \(P(Y>1 \mid X>1)=1\) while \(P(Y>1)=0.3173\). Symmetry alone fails for \(X=+1\) or \(-1\) with probability 1/2 each: then \(Y=1\) is constant and independent of \(X\).

selfTest.q: In Reproduce, which part of 12.0208 comes from within-branch variation and which from between-branch variation?
selfTest.a: \(35/24=1.4583\) is \(\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X \mid \text{branch})]\), the within part, all of it from the die since the constant branch has zero variance. \((10-3.5)^2/4=10.5625\) is \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X \mid \text{branch}])\), the between part.

selfTest.q: Why does the reproduce check quote 0.00548 alongside the mean?
selfTest.a: It is the simulation standard error, \(\mathrm{sd}/\sqrt{n}\). Without it the comparison of 6.7493 against 6.75 has no scale; agreement means within a few standard errors.

study.title: Distribution families and change of variables
study.locator: Chapter 2, Sections 2.4-2.6 (pp. 49-61) for Bernoulli, categorical and Gaussian; Sections 2.8.3-2.8.5 (pp. 67-72) for bijections, the Jacobian factor and convolutions

focus: Tie each family to a sampling story: counts of trials, waiting times, arrivals per interval. The story selects the family; the data never does by itself.
A change of variables multiplies by the Jacobian absolute determinant and re-derives the support. A density without a support is unfinished.
Sums of independent variables convolve densities; MGFs turn convolution into multiplication where the MGF exists near zero.
Parametrization traps: Exponential and Gamma rate versus scale, Normal variance versus standard deviation. State yours in every signature.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive by the CDF method that \(U \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) gives \(X=-\log(U) \sim \operatorname{Expo}(1)\): \(P(X \le x)=P(U \ge e^{-x})=1-e^{-x}\) for \(x \ge 0\), using continuity of \(U\) for the strict-inequality step. Then check with NumPy in float64: numpy.random.default_rng(31), 300000 draws via random() then -log; sample mean 0.9983 and variance 1.0024 against exact 1 and 1, and \(P(X>2)=0.1341\) against exact \(e^{-2}=0.1353\) with standard error 0.00062.
traps: Dropping the Jacobian factor or keeping the old support after a transform. Both silently produce a function that does not integrate to 1.
Assuming every distribution has an MGF. Cauchy has none; quote the MGF only with its domain.
Confusing Poisson counts with Exponential waiting times. They describe one process from two sides; the units differ.

selfTest.q: Derive the density of \(Y=X^2\) for \(X \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(-1, 1)\), naming the non-monotone step.
selfTest.a: \(F_Y(y)=P(-\sqrt{y} \le X \le \sqrt{y})=\sqrt{y}\) on \((0,1)\), using the two-sided preimage; differentiating gives \(f_Y(y)=1/(2\sqrt{y})\) on \((0,1)\). The monotone CDF rule applied to one branch alone would halve the answer.

selfTest.q: Why does Box-Muller produce two independent Normals from two Uniforms?
selfTest.a: The polar map \((U_1, U_2) \to (R\cos, R\sin)\) with \(R^2=-2\log U_1\) has Jacobian factor that splits the joint density into a product of two standard Normal densities. Independence is read off the factored form.

selfTest.q: \(X \sim \operatorname{Pois}(2)\) counts arrivals per hour and \(T \sim \operatorname{Expo}(2)\) is the wait for the next arrival. Are \(X\) and \(T\) the same object?
selfTest.a: No. \(X\) is discrete with mean 2; \(T\) is continuous with mean 1/2 hour. Same rate parameter, different sample spaces and different questions.

selfTest.q: In Reproduce, why is random() with -log enough, and what would break with integers(0, 2)?
selfTest.a: Inverse-CDF needs a continuous \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) input so that \(P(U \ge u)=1-u\); the proof step uses continuity. A discrete input would quantize \(X\) and the CDF derivation would fail. random() can also return exactly 0.0 (probability \(2^{-53}\) per draw), so library samplers use -log1p(-U) on the same input.

study.title: Beta-Binomial posterior and posterior predictive
study.locator: Chapter 4, Sections 4.6.1-4.6.2.10 (pp. 129-136): conjugate priors, Beta-Binomial posterior, MAP, posterior predictive and marginal likelihood
study.depth: Stop before Section 4.6.2.11 (mixtures of conjugate priors). The Dirichlet and Gaussian models and the computation methods of Section 4.6.8 belong to later stages.

focus: Conjugacy is algebra: a Beta prior times a Binomial likelihood is Beta up to a constant. The update adds successes to \(a\) and failures to \(b\).
The posterior predictive averages over the posterior; the plug-in forecast conditions on one estimate. They differ most with little data.
The evidence normalizes the posterior for fixed data and compares models across hypotheses. It never rescales a single posterior's shape.
A graphical factorization is a chain-rule product with dropped conditioning bars. Each dropped bar is a conditional-independence claim to defend.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the Beta-Binomial update for a \(\operatorname{Beta}(2, 2)\) prior with 7 heads in 10 flips: posterior \(\operatorname{Beta}(9, 5)\), mean \(9/14=0.6429\), MAP \(8/12=0.6667\), posterior predictive \(P(\text{next head})=9/14\). Check with NumPy in float64: numpy.random.default_rng(41), 300000 beta(9, 5) draws; posterior mean 0.6430 with standard error 0.00023, one binomial(1, theta) flip per draw from the same generator gives predictive fraction 0.6439, and the 2.5 and 97.5 percent sample quantiles give the 95 percent credible interval [0.385, 0.862] (exact \(\operatorname{Beta}(9, 5)\) quantiles 0.386 and 0.861).
traps: Reporting the MAP as the posterior mean. For a \(\operatorname{Beta}(a, b)\) posterior they coincide only when \(a=b\); here 0.6667 differs from 0.6429.
Reading a 95 percent credible interval as a 95 percent confidence interval. One conditions on the observed data with a prior; the other is a pre-data coverage statement.
Reusing the same data to pick the prior and to update. That double counts the evidence; run a prior-sensitivity check instead.

selfTest.q: Derive the \(\operatorname{Beta}(9, 5)\) posterior from Bayes rule and name the step that uses conjugacy.
selfTest.a: Posterior is proportional to \(\theta^7(1-\theta)^3\) times \(\theta^1(1-\theta)^1=\theta^8(1-\theta)^4\). Recognizing this kernel as \(\operatorname{Beta}(9, 5)\) up to its normalizing constant is the conjugacy step; it uses the Beta integral identity.

selfTest.q: Derive the posterior predictive 9/14 and state the assumption that lets the integral close.
selfTest.a: \(P(\text{next head} \mid \text{data})\) = integral of \(\theta\) times \(\operatorname{Beta}(9, 5)\) = \(\mathbb{E}[\theta]=9/14\). The integral closes because the Bernoulli likelihood is linear in \(\theta\) and the posterior is Beta; exchangeability of the flips justifies reusing the same \(\theta\).

selfTest.q: How does the predictive probability move if the prior changes from \(\operatorname{Beta}(2, 2)\) to \(\operatorname{Beta}(20, 20)\) with the same 7-in-10 data?
selfTest.a: The posterior becomes \(\operatorname{Beta}(27, 23)\) with mean \(27/50=0.54\), pulled from 0.6429 toward the prior mean 0.5. Sensitivity shrinks as data grow: the prior contributes a fixed pseudo-count (40 here) against \(n\) real trials.

selfTest.q: A two-node graph \(X \to Y\) claims \(p(x, y)=p(x)p(y \mid x)\). What does the missing bar encode?
selfTest.a: Nothing is dropped here: it is the chain rule. A claim appears only with more parents or missing edges, for example \(p(y \mid x, z)=p(y \mid x)\), which asserts \(Y\) is independent of \(Z\) given \(X\).

study.title: CLT and Monte Carlo approximation
study.locator: Chapter 2, Sections 2.8.6-2.8.7 (pp. 72-73): central limit behavior and the Monte Carlo approximation of a distribution

focus: Each bound buys generality with looseness: Markov needs only non-negativity, Chebyshev adds a finite variance, Hoeffding adds bounded independent summands.
The CLT describes the standardized mean, not the raw sum and not the underlying distribution. \(n = 30\) is folklore, not a theorem.
Monte Carlo error scales as \(1/\sqrt{n}\): one more decimal digit costs 100 times the samples. Quote every estimate with its standard error.
Dependence and heavy tails break the standard bars. An MCMC-style correlated stream or a Cauchy average needs its own analysis.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute exact \(P(|Z|>2)=2(1-\Phi(2))=0.045500\) for \(Z \sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, 1)\) via the error function, then check three claims with NumPy in float64: numpy.random.default_rng(51), 400000 standard_normal draws give tail fraction 0.04596 with standard error 0.00033; Chebyshev allows \(P(|Z|>2) \le 1/4=0.25\), loose but valid since \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=1\); Hoeffding gives \(P(|\hat{p}-p| \ge 0.05) \le 2\exp(-10)=9.08 \times 10^{-5}\) for 2000 independent fair-coin flips.
traps: Reading a bound as an approximation. Chebyshev's 0.25 against the true 0.0455 is a guarantee, not a prediction.
Applying Hoeffding to dependent or unbounded summands. Independence and boundedness enter the proof; dropping either voids it.
Judging convergence from one sample size. Halve the observed standard error across a 4x sample-size run before claiming \(1/\sqrt{n}\) scaling.

selfTest.q: Prove Chebyshev from Markov and name the step that needs a finite variance.
selfTest.a: \(P(|X-\mu| \ge k\sigma)=P((X-\mu)^2 \ge k^2\sigma^2) \le \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]/(k^2\sigma^2)=1/k^2\). Markov needs a non-negative variable, supplied by squaring; finiteness of \(\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]\) is the variance assumption.

selfTest.q: Why is Hoeffding's 9.08e-05 far below Chebyshev-style bounds for the coin example, and what does it cost?
selfTest.a: Hoeffding exploits bounded independent summands to get exponential tails, while Chebyshev uses only variance for \(1/k^2\) tails. The cost is the stronger assumption: boundedness plus full independence.

selfTest.q: Averages of 100 Cauchy draws still jump around. Which assumption fails for the LLN and the CLT?
selfTest.a: Finite mean for the LLN and finite variance for the CLT. Cauchy has neither, so neither theorem applies; the sample mean stays Cauchy at every n.

selfTest.q: Your Monte Carlo tail estimate at \(n=400000\) gives 0.04596 with SE 0.00033. How many draws for SE 0.0001?
selfTest.a: About \((0.00033/0.0001)^2=11\) times more, roughly 4.4 million draws. Standard error scales as \(1/\sqrt{n}\), so a 3.3x reduction needs an 11x sample.

study.title: Entropy, KL non-negativity and mutual information
study.locator: Chapter 6, Sections 6.1-6.2 and 6.3.1-6.3.4 (pp. 207-220): entropy and chain rules, Theorem 6.2.1 (\(\mathrm{KL} \ge 0\) by Jensen), KL versus maximum likelihood, mutual information identities

focus: \(\mathrm{CE}(P, Q)=H(P)+\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)\). Fitting \(Q\) moves only the KL term; \(H(P)\) is constant for fixed data.
KL direction matters: \(\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)\) punishes \(Q\) near zero where \(P\) is positive, even infinite for a hard zero. Averaging the wrong direction answers a different question.

Log base sets the units: base 2 gives bits, base e gives nats, and 1 nat = 1.4427 bits. ProbML Chapter 6 and the D2L entropy helpers use base 2; the D2L cross-entropy loss and PyTorch losses use base e. Convert before comparing.
Mutual information \(I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X \mid Y)\) is zero exactly under independence. Correlation only sees linear dependence; MI sees any.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute in bits for \(P=(0.5, 0.25, 0.25)\) against uniform \(Q\) over 3 outcomes: \(H(P)=1.5\), \(\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)=0.0850\), \(\mathrm{CE}(P, Q)=1.5850\), and \(\mathrm{CE}=H+\mathrm{KL}\) term by term. Check with NumPy in float64 using log2: \(H=1.5000\), \(\mathrm{KL}=0.0850\), \(\mathrm{CE}=1.5850\), with agreement of \(\mathrm{CE}\) and \(H+\mathrm{KL}\) to 1e-12 in absolute value.
traps: Calling KL a distance. It is asymmetric and violates the triangle inequality: for the Reproduce pair, \(\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)=0.0850\) bits but \(\mathrm{KL}(Q\|P)=0.0817\) bits.
Taking abs() around a KL implementation, as the D2L helper does. A negative KL signals a bug (unnormalized inputs or swapped logs); abs hides it.
Assuming differential entropy is non-negative. Continuous entropy can be negative; only the discrete form \(H \ge 0\) holds.

selfTest.q: Prove \(\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q) \ge 0\) for discrete distributions and name the step that uses each assumption.
selfTest.a: \(\mathrm{KL}=\mathbb{E}_P[-\log(q/p)] \ge -\log(\mathbb{E}_P[q/p])\) by Jensen for the convex \(-\log\); the expectation step needs \(p\) a valid PMF. \(\mathbb{E}_P[q/p]\) = sum over support of \(P\) of \(q \le 1\), with equality iff supports match; \(-\log\) of that is \(\ge 0\), using \(q\) a valid PMF. Equality needs \(q=p\) on the support of \(P\).

selfTest.q: In Reproduce, which term changes if \(Q\) is fitted to \(P\), and what is its minimum?
selfTest.a: Only \(\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)\) changes; \(H(P)=1.5\) is fixed by the data. Its minimum is 0, attained at \(Q=P\), where CE equals \(H(P)\).

selfTest.q: \(Q\) assigns 0 to an outcome with \(P=0.25\). What happens to \(\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)\) and to a Monte Carlo CE estimate?
selfTest.a: KL is infinite: the term \(0.25\log(0.25/0)\) diverges. A finite sample avoiding that outcome still estimates finite CE, which hides the infinite population KL. Support mismatch is a modeling error, not a sampling artifact.

selfTest.q: \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent bits. What are \(H(X \mid Y)\) and \(I(X;Y)\)?
selfTest.a: \(H(X \mid Y)=H(X)\) since conditioning on \(Y\) removes nothing; \(I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X \mid Y)=0\). Independence zeroes mutual information in both directions.
